Rest of Today through Wednesday...

Warm and dry conditions this afternoon with periods of clouds
pushing through from southwest to northeast. Afternoon
temperatures will be well into the mid 70s with a few locations
close to 80 degrees by 4pm. 

Storm System late tonight through Saturday morning...Changes from
the recent warm and dry pattern begin late tonight as an upper 
level low over the Great Basin pushes this direction throwing 
increased moisture over the area, and a Canadian trof slides in 
from the northwest bringing colder air and additional upper level 
support for precipitation. The good news is models have
consolidated their thinking over the past 24 hours and the
forecast has stabilized, so no big changes with this forecast
package. 

Expect showers, and possibly an isolated thunderstorm, to build 
into southwest mountain/foothills zones overnight and into the 
sunrise period. Main front will push into northwest zones around 
noon with a good deal of wind (gusts 30-45 mph with a few lower 
50s here and there) behind it thanks to 2-3mb/hr pressure rises 
behind the front. The strongest winds are expected from mid
afternoon through late Friday night. Precipitation will fill in 
along and behind the front with high chances for the western 2/3 
of the area through Friday evening. Eastern zones still look to 
get left out of significant precipitation with this system, but 
there is still a 15-30% chance for a shower/thunderstorm late 
afternoon into the evening hours. Overall, the bulk of 
precipitation will be done by midnight Friday night with chances 
diminishing through sunrise as the upper level energy splits north
and south of the area leaving just some lingering gusty winds and
much cooler temperatures for Saturday. 

Rainfall forecast shows the probability for a quarter inch or more
in the 30 to 50 percent range west of a Roundup to Hardin line,
with 60-100 percent west of a Ryegate to Big Timber line and into
the Western mountains. From Rosebud county east the probabilities
for a tenth of an inch of precipitation are under 20 percent, and
near zero for most of Carter and Fallon counties. 

No significant changes to the snowfall forecast this afternoon. 
Still looking at a dusting in the western foothills with 4 to 8 
inches in the Beartooth/Absaroka/Crazy mountains, and 4 inches or 
less for the Bighorn and Pryor mountains. Snow levels fall to
under 4kft after 3am Friday night, so there could be a few flakes
mixed in across the lower elevations down to 3200ft as
precipitation is tapering off early Saturday morning, but do not
expect any impactful snowfall (>1 in) outside of the western 
foothills above around 5kft. 

Will issue a Winter Weather Advisory for the Judith Gap zone for 
late Friday afternoon through 6am Saturday. Strong northerly winds
will combine with snowfall there (2 inches or less) to make 
travel difficult along US-191 from Harlowton up through Judith 
Gap. Heaviest snow will be in the 8pm through 2am range and wind
gusts 40-55 mph will create poor visibility in blowing snow. Roads
will be mainly slushy overnight, but some slick snow covered spots
can be expected especially over the higher hills along this route. 

Fire Weather...Ahead of the front over NC WY/SE MT south-
southwest winds gusting 30 to 40 mph will develop and persist 
until the front arrives early evening. Post frontal winds will 
shift to the northwest with gusts to 45 mph through the early 
morning hours. Afternoon temperatures in this area will range from
75 to 85 degrees (20-30 degrees above normal), in the record high
temperature range for the day. RH values will drop into the 
15-25% range as well. So, this sets up as a critical weather 
scenario for grass fire danger from Sheridan county east along the
MT/WY state line. Will issue a Red Flag Warning for Friday 
afternoon through 9pm Friday evening for the Sheridan foothills 
and a good portion of SE Montana to cover this scenario. 

Storm system dissipates Saturday afternoon for a seasonally cool
and breezy afternoon. 

The next concern is another upper low moving northeast from the 
Great Basin and clipping SE Montana late Sunday into Monday. 
Models are steadily ramping up precipitation chances (20-40%) for 
this area. Right on the heals of the Great Basin system, a
stronger and more organized Pacific system pushes into the area
from the west for Tuesday and Wednesday with more widespread
30-50% precipitation chances. Lates model runs are tapping some
colder air with this system by Wednesday along with better upslope
flow into north facing mountains/foothills than previously
advertised, so precipitation chances could continue to rise with
this system going forward, and may see chances for lower elevation
snowfall mix in too. As mentioned yesterday there is still
considerable uncertainty with the forecast for next week so stay
tuned to the forecast as details get ironed out going forward.
Chambers
